market_context: United States; postharvest browning and household storage of lettuce.
title: Why Lettuce Turns Brown

seo.title: Why Lettuce Turns Brown
seo.meta_description: Cuts and bruises trigger phenolic metabolism that forms brown pigments; ethylene can also cause russet spotting. Cold storage and gentle handling slow these changes.
seo.search_intent: Understand lettuce browning and distinguish physiological discoloration from decay.

excerpt: Lettuce can turn brown for several reasons. Cutting and bruising stimulate phenolic metabolism that produces dark pigments, while ethylene from apples, pears, and other ripe fruit can trigger brown russet spotting. These physiological defects are different from bacterial rot or mold.
content_html:
Fresh-cut lettuce can develop brown edges before it is actually spoiled. Browning often begins as a tissue response to injury and oxygen.

Cutting activates phenolic metabolism

UC Davis explains that damaged and cut lettuce develops pink or brown discoloration through wound-induced phenolic metabolism. More crushing means more injured tissue and more opportunity for discoloration.

Ethylene can create brown spots too

Lettuce is very sensitive to ethylene. Exposure around 1 ppm can produce russet spotting, especially on veins and ribs. Storing lettuce near apples, pears, or other ripe ethylene-producing fruit can accelerate the defect.

Brown does not always mean unsafe

A dry brown edge or a few physiological spots are mainly quality problems. Slime, watery breakdown, rotten odor, and mold are stronger spoilage signals.

A brown edge and a slimy leaf do not tell the same story

Browning after cutting can be a localized enzymatic response that mainly affects appearance. When lettuce loses structure, leaks liquid, becomes slimy or develops an unpleasant smell, deterioration is much further advanced. Looking at the whole leaf avoids using a single color as a diagnosis.

Clean cutting tools, cold storage and less mechanical damage slow some of these reactions. Cut lettuce still ages faster than an intact head because much more tissue surface is exposed.

How to slow browning

  • Keep lettuce well refrigerated.
  • Cut close to serving time.
  • Use a sharp knife and avoid crushing.
  • Store away from strong ethylene producers.
  • Avoid condensation and free water.

Color can be cosmetic; slimy texture and rotten odor tell you much more about true deterioration.

The pattern of browning can point to the cause

A cut edge that slowly turns tan or brown usually fits mechanical injury followed by phenolic oxidation. Small russet or brown speckles can have a different trigger: lettuce is sensitive to ethylene, especially when stored near produce such as apples, pears, or bananas. These discolorations may look similar at first glance, but they do not necessarily develop through the same pathway.

Moisture needs balance as well. Leaves that remain wet for long periods can deteriorate and become slimy faster, while leaves that lose too much water wilt and lose crispness. Cold storage with limited surface moisture and some way to manage condensation works better than sealing dripping-wet lettuce in a container. A clean paper towel can help absorb excess moisture when needed.

If lettuce is washed before storage, drying it thoroughly matters. A salad spinner removes surface water without crushing the leaves. For an intact head that will be used gradually, washing only what is needed can sometimes preserve texture longer, unless the product was sold prewashed and ready to eat.

Color alone is not a complete spoilage test. Dry brown edges can often be trimmed when the remaining leaves smell normal and stay crisp. Widespread slime, mold, a distinctly unpleasant odor, or major tissue breakdown are different signs and are better reasons to discard the lettuce. This distinction helps prevent wasting edible leaves while still recognizing genuine deterioration.

Knife choice is less magical than it is sometimes presented, but a clean cut damages less tissue than crushing or tearing the leaf aggressively. A sharp blade can leave neater edges for short-term preparation. Over several days, however, temperature, moisture management, and ethylene exposure have a much larger effect on how quickly the lettuce loses quality.

Cut lettuce also deteriorates faster than an intact head because more tissue is wounded and exposed. Preparing salads well in advance is convenient, but maximum crispness usually comes from keeping the leaves cold, dry, and undressed until close to serving. Acidic dressing, salt, and mechanical tossing all change water movement and texture once the salad is assembled.

If a packaged salad has a use-by date and specific storage instructions, those directions matter in addition to visual quality. Browning can be harmless, but date and temperature controls address risks that cannot always be seen.

Browning should also be separated from wilting. A leaf can remain green yet become limp because it has lost water, while another can have a dry brown edge and still be crisp. Briefly soaking wilted lettuce in very cold water may restore some turgor, but it will not reverse slimy tissue or microbial spoilage. Texture and odor therefore provide useful context that color alone cannot supply.

faq.question: Can I eat lettuce with brown edges?
faq.answer: Yes if the lettuce is otherwise crisp and normal with no mold, slime, or rotten odor.

faq.question: Can apples make lettuce brown?
faq.answer: They can contribute because apples release ethylene and lettuce is highly sensitive to it.

faq.question: Does cutting cause browning?
faq.answer: Yes. Cutting wounds the tissue and activates reactions that form colored phenolic compounds.
